place.en: Black Pine Ridge · the stream at the valley mouth

setup.zh: 那头鹿还在谷口的溪边喝水：三百步，东北，顺风。明天就是立冬。爹站不起来，把爷爷的弓递给了你。
setup.en: The deer is still drinking at the stream by the valley mouth: three hundred paces, northeast, downwind. Tomorrow is the Start of Winter. Father cannot stand; he gives you grandfather's bow.

recap.zh: 你拉开爷爷的弓射中了那头雄鹿；银月撑着说完指路的话，晕了过去。
recap.en: You drew grandfather's bow and brought down the stag; Yinyue held on long enough to guide the shot, and fainted.

zh: 一头雄鹿低头饮水，角如枯枝。
en: A stag drinks, antlers like dead branches.
The bow is heavier than you thought.

story.zh:
一行人正要下山，银月忽然在小满耳边开了口。

⟪「那头鹿。」⟫

她的声音比方才更小了：「谷口……溪边……在喝水。三百步，东北，顺风。」

小满低声道：「你怎么知道？」「本王是妖王。」「你方才说，醒一回，薄一分——」她没接这话，只道：「……本王欠你一张饼。先还个利息。」

他拉了拉他爹的袖子，朝东北指了一指，道：「爹，有鹿。」老周拦他：「你那腿——」他爹道：「明天立冬。」

溪边一头雄鹿正低着头喝水。他爹搭上了箭，要站起来——却站不起来。小满低声道：「爹，让我来。」他爹看着他。看了很久。然后他把爷爷的弓，递给了儿子。

那弓比小满想的沉得多。他搭上箭，往后拉。拉到一半，胳膊便开始打颤。

他爹在身后轻声道：「先看风。」小满看风。他等着。胳膊在抖，手腕在疼，那头鹿喝饱了水，随时都要走。他还是等着。风过去了，芦草晃了两晃，慢慢地直起来——
story.en:
The party was just about to head down the mountain when Yinyue suddenly spoke in Xiaoman's ear.

⟪"That deer."⟫

Her voice was smaller than before: "Mouth of the valley… by the stream… drinking. Three hundred paces, north-east, downwind."

Xiaoman stopped mid-step. "How do you know?" "This queen is a demon queen." "You just said every time you wake you wear thinner—" She didn't answer that. She only said, "…This queen owes you one flatbread. Here's some of the interest first."

He tugged his father's sleeve and pointed north-east. "Pa, there's a deer." Old Zhou tried to stop him: "Your leg—" His father said, "Tomorrow's the first day of winter."

At the edge of the stream a stag stood with its head down, drinking. His father nocked an arrow and went to stand up — and couldn't. Xiaoman said quietly, "Pa, let me." His father looked at him. Looked at him a long time. Then he handed Grandpa's bow to his son.

The bow was much heavier than Xiaoman had thought. He nocked the arrow and drew. Halfway, his arm began to shake.

Behind him his father said softly, "First read the wind." Xiaoman read the wind. He waited. His arm was shaking, his wrist was hurting, and the stag had drunk its fill and might go at any moment. He kept waiting. The gust passed; the reeds wavered twice and slowly rose —

story_full.zh:
一行人正要下山，银月忽然在小满耳边开了口。

⟪「那头鹿。」⟫

她的声音比方才更小了，小得像一根线，一口气倒像要分成三口来说：「谷口……溪边……在喝水。三百步，东北，顺风。」

小满脚下一顿，低声道：「你怎么知道？」

「本王是妖王。」

「你方才说，醒一回，薄一分——」

她没接这话，只道：「……本王欠你一张饼。先还个利息。」

小满心里一跳。昨儿晌午他爹在山涧边上摸着的那个蹄印，便是往东北去的。立冬，是明天。

他拉了拉他爹的袖子，朝东北指了一指，道：「爹，有鹿。」

老周在旁道：「什么鹿？你怎么知道它在那边？」小满想起银月那句「本王只肯让你看见」，便拔了一根草，举在半空。那草尖儿往他们身后歪，风是从东北吹过来的。他道：「风从那边来，带着一股骚味。是鹿。」

其实他什么味儿也没闻见。可他爹是闻了一辈子风的人，听儿子这么一说，也仰起脸来，抽了抽鼻子，闻了很久，才低声道：「……是有。」那一刻他爹是当真闻见了，还是不肯让儿子的话落了空，只怕他爹自己也说不清。

老周拦他：「你那腿——」他爹道：「明天立冬。」老周便不拦了，自己跟了上来。

三人摸过去。老周踩断了一根枯枝，挨了一眼，便把两只鞋脱了，拎在手里，光着脚走。走满三百步，只听得水声潺潺，小满拨开枝叶往外一看，溪边一头雄鹿正低着头喝水。

小满这辈子没见过那样的鹿。它比他家那扇门还高，一身赭红的毛，太阳底下亮得像一块缎子，头上那对角，像一丛冬天的枯树枝。

他爹搭上了箭，要站起来——却站不起来。那条左腿在坡上趴了一夜，又在崖上吊了半晌，他撑着地使了两回劲，膝盖只是「咯」地响了一声。他想跪着射，左膝一沾地，整张脸便白了。

小满低声道：「爹，让我来。」

他爹看着他。看了很久，久到那头鹿又低下头去喝了两口水。然后他把爷爷的弓，递给了儿子。

那弓比小满想的沉得多。

弓背上缠的牛筋他数过，十七道，跟家里的盆一样多，可他从来没有拉过它。左手一握弓把，那只肿着的手腕疼得他眼前一黑。他把那口气咽了回去，搭上箭，往后拉。

拉到一半，胳膊便开始打颤，颤得那支箭在弓背上一跳一跳的。他又往后拉了一寸，左手腕里「喀」的一声轻响，一股酸疼顺着胳膊里侧，一直窜到了肩窝。

他爹在身后轻声道：「先看风。」

小满看风。溪边的芦草一阵往这边倒，一阵又直起来。他等着。胳膊在抖，手腕在疼，那头鹿喝饱了水，随时都要走。他还是等着。风过去了，芦草晃了两晃，慢慢地直起来——
story_full.en:
The party was just about to head down the mountain when Yinyue suddenly spoke in Xiaoman's ear.

⟪"That deer."⟫

Her voice was smaller than before, as thin as a thread, as if one breath had to be split into three to get the words out: "Mouth of the valley… by the stream… drinking. Three hundred paces, north-east, downwind."

Xiaoman stopped mid-step. "How do you know?" he whispered.

"This queen is a demon queen."

"You just said every time you wake you wear thinner—"

She didn't answer that. She only said, "…This queen owes you one flatbread. Here's some of the interest first."

Xiaoman's heart leapt. The hoof print his father had touched by the mountain stream yesterday noon had been heading north-east. The first day of winter was tomorrow.

He tugged his father's sleeve and pointed north-east. "Pa, there's a deer."

Old Zhou, standing by, said, "What deer? How do you know it's over there?" Xiaoman remembered Yinyue's "This queen lets only you see", so he pulled a blade of grass and held it up. The tip leaned back past them; the wind was coming from the north-east. He said, "Wind's from over there, and there's a musky smell on it. It's a deer."

In fact he couldn't smell a thing. But his father had been smelling the wind all his life, and when he heard his son say this he lifted his face too, sniffed, sniffed for a long time, and then said quietly, "…There is." Whether at that moment his father had really smelled it, or just wouldn't let his son's words fall flat, even his father probably couldn't have said.

Old Zhou tried to stop him: "Your leg—" His father said, "Tomorrow's the first day of winter." Old Zhou stopped trying, and came along himself.

The three of them crept over. Old Zhou stepped on a dry twig and snapped it, got a look for it, and took off both his shoes, carrying them in his hand and going barefoot. After a full three hundred paces they heard the babble of water. Xiaoman parted the leaves and looked out: at the edge of the stream a stag stood with its head down, drinking.

Xiaoman had never in his life seen a deer like it. It was taller than his family's door, with a coat of reddish-brown that shone like satin in the sun, and on its head a pair of antlers like a clump of bare winter branches.

His father nocked an arrow and went to stand up — and couldn't. That left leg had spent a night lying on the slope and then a good while hanging on the cliff. He pushed against the ground twice, and the knee only gave a *click*. He tried to shoot kneeling, but the moment his left knee touched the ground his whole face went white.

Xiaoman said quietly, "Pa, let me." His father looked at him.

Looked at him a long time, long enough for the stag to lower its head and drink twice more. Then he handed Grandpa's bow to his son.

The bow was much heavier than Xiaoman had thought.

He'd counted the turns of ox sinew on its back — seventeen, as many as the basins at home — but he had never drawn it. The moment his left hand closed on the grip, his swollen wrist hurt so much everything went black. He swallowed the breath back down, nocked the arrow and drew.

Halfway, his arm began to shake, shaking so that the arrow jumped against the bow. He drew another inch, and something in his left wrist gave a small *crick*; an aching pain shot up the inside of his arm right into the hollow of his shoulder.

Behind him his father said softly, "First read the wind."

Xiaoman read the wind. The reeds along the stream leaned this way for a moment, then stood up again. He waited. His arm was shaking, his wrist was hurting, and the stag had drunk its fill and might go at any moment. He kept waiting. The gust passed; the reeds wavered twice and slowly rose —

label.en: Half an inch to the left

exits.means: aims a little left for the wind, as told, and shoots

story.zh:
便在这时，银月在他耳边道：⟪「往左偏半寸。」⟫小满往左偏了半寸。芦草将直未直。他手指一松。

那箭已离弦而去，他还没瞧清它飞到了哪里，只觉得肩膀上一轻。那只小银狐从他脖子上滑了下来。他扔了弓，一把把它接住了——它闭着眼睛，身子凉得像一块冰。他想说「谢了」，那句话已经到了舌头尖上，可它闭着眼睛，听不见了。

溪边那头鹿却没有倒。三个人顺着溪往下走。弯里的浅滩上，那头鹿侧躺着，那支箭正中它的脖子，不偏不倚。他爹扑通一声跪在鹿旁边，回过头来看儿子，笑得像个孩子。

老周瞧瞧那头鹿，又瞧瞧小满，道：「一箭？」小满他爹道：「一箭。」老周道：「他才十二。」他爹道：「我十四才摸这张弓。我爹也是十四。」他低下头去，又道：「他十二。」

那副门板，到底没有白扛，抬了一头鹿。小满走在最后，背着弓，捂着胸口。胸口那团东西，一路上一回也没动过。

围上来看鹿的人堆后头，刘豆芽看了那头鹿一眼，一转身，往马家那边跑了。他娘走到儿子跟前，从自己衣襟底下撕下一条干净的布，一圈一圈，重新给他缠上。然后她转过身去，看小满他爹。她伸手，从他肩膀上拈掉了一根松针。

那天夜里，马小宝在井台边上拦住阿禾，拿一块桂花糕换话：「刘豆芽说，沈家抬回来一头大鹿。真有那么大？」阿禾道：「他看岔了。一头小母鹿，瘸了一条腿。要不然，沈小满射得着？」老周一把夺过那块糕，往篱笆外一扔：「明儿马三一看是头大公鹿，你这张嘴，就是沈家的祸！」
story.en:
And just then Yinyue said in his ear, ⟪"Half an inch to the left."⟫ Xiaoman moved half an inch left. The reeds were nearly upright but not quite. His fingers let go.

The arrow was off the string with a *whoosh*, and before he could see where it went, his shoulder suddenly felt light. The little silver fox slid off his neck and dropped, limp. He threw down the bow and caught it — its eyes were shut, its body cold as a lump of ice. He wanted to say "thanks". The words were already on the tip of his tongue, but its eyes were shut, and it couldn't hear any more.

The stag by the stream, though, didn't fall. The three of them went down along the stream. On the shallows in the bend the stag lay on its side, the arrow right through its neck, dead on the mark. His father dropped to his knees beside the deer with a thump, and turned round to look at his son, grinning like a child.

Old Zhou looked at the deer, then at Xiaoman. "One arrow?" Xiaoman's father said, "One arrow." Old Zhou said, "He's only twelve." His father said, "I didn't touch this bow till I was fourteen. Nor did my father." He bent his head. Then he said, "He's twelve."

The door hadn't been lugged up for nothing after all: it carried a deer. Xiaoman walked last, bow on his back, hand on his chest. The thing against his chest didn't move once the whole way.

At the back of the crowd that gathered round to look at the deer, Beansprout Liu took one look at it, turned, and ran off towards the Ma place. His mother came up to her son. She tore a clean strip from under the hem of her own jacket, and wrapped it on again, round and round. Then she turned and looked at Xiaoman's father. She reached out and picked a pine needle off his shoulder.

That night Ma Xiaobao stopped Ahe by the well platform and traded her a piece of osmanthus cake for talk. "Beansprout Liu says the Shens brought back a great big deer. Was it really that big?" Ahe said, "He saw wrong. A little doe with a lame leg. Otherwise how could Shen Xiaoman have hit it?" Old Zhou snatched the cake from her and threw it over the fence. "Tomorrow when Ma San sees it's a big stag, that mouth of yours will be the ruin of the Shens!"

story_full.zh:
便在这时，银月在他耳边道：⟪「往左偏半寸。」⟫

她的声音很轻，很累，像是从很远很远的地方飘过来的。小满往左偏了半寸。

芦草将直未直。他手指一松。

那箭已离弦而去，「嗖」的一声，他还没瞧清它飞到了哪里，只觉得肩膀上一轻。那只小银狐从他脖子上滑了下来，软软地往下掉。他扔了弓，一把把它接住了——它闭着眼睛，身子凉得像一块冰。昨儿夜里它是烫的，烫的至少还是活的。小满慌了，把它往怀里一塞，贴着胸口捂着，觉出它很慢、很慢地，还在喘气。

他张了张嘴。他想说「谢了」，或者「谢谢你」，或者别的什么，总之是一句带「谢」字的话。那句话已经到了舌头尖上，可它闭着眼睛，听不见了。

溪边那头鹿却没有倒。它脖子上挂着那支箭，猛地一跃，蹿过了溪，一头扎进对岸的林子里去了。他爹一把拽住要追的老周：「别追。追，它跑得更远。」说着闭上了眼睛，听了一袋烟的工夫，才道：「它跑不动了。顺着溪，往下走，二百步，有个弯。」

三个人顺着溪往下走。走满二百步，溪水拐了一个弯，弯里的浅滩上，那头鹿侧躺着，那支箭正中它的脖子，不偏不倚。它是跑到这里，才倒下的。

他爹一瘸一拐地跑过去，跑得比老周还快，扑通一声跪在鹿旁边——膝盖也顾不得了——伸手去摸那对角，回过头来看儿子，笑得像个孩子。

小满也笑。可他的手一直按在胸口上，没敢松开。

老周瞧瞧那头鹿，又瞧瞧小满，道：「一箭？」小满他爹道：「一箭。」老周道：「他才十二。」他爹道：「我十四才摸这张弓。我爹也是十四。」他低下头去，拿手掌一下一下地摸着那头鹿的脖子，又道：「他十二。」

他没有再说别的。可他说那三个字的腔调，和他跟马三说「三爷」的腔调，是不一样的。

那副门板，到底没有白扛，抬了一头鹿。他爹非要抬后头，谁劝也不听。小满走在最后，背着弓，捂着胸口。胸口那团东西，一路上一回也没动过。

到得村口，已是傍晚。

老槐树底下，站着两个人。一个是阿禾，两只脚尖齐齐地抵在老槐树的树根上，身子却往前探着，脖子伸得像一只等食的鹅——她娘不让她出村口，老槐树就是村口。她一只脚也没出去，脖子却已经出去了。

另一个站在老槐树底下的，是小满他娘。她从前一日天黑一直站到这一日傍晚，中间只回过一趟家，给灶里添了一把火——万一人回来了，灶是凉的，那可不行。

围上来看鹿的人堆后头，刘豆芽看了那头鹿一眼，一转身，往马家那边跑了。

他娘走到儿子跟前，先看他的脸，又看他那只肿着的左手腕，腕上缠着半片衣摆，早给泥水泡成了一条烂布。她一句话也没说，把那条烂布解了下来，从自己衣襟底下撕下一条干净的布，一圈一圈，重新给他缠上，打了一个结，方方正正，跟她补衣裳打的结一模一样。

然后她转过身去，看小满他爹。他爹抬着门板的后头，脸上的泥还没洗，一双眼睛红得像兔子。两个人对看了一眼，谁也没说话。她伸手，从他肩膀上拈掉了一根松针。

就这么一下。

那天夜里，马小宝在井台边上拦住阿禾，拿一块桂花糕换话：「刘豆芽说，沈家抬回来一头大鹿。真有那么大？」阿禾道：「他看岔了。一头小母鹿，瘸了一条腿。要不然，沈小满射得着？」马小宝觉得十分有理，把糕往她手里一塞，走了。老周从门里抢出来，一把夺过那块糕，往篱笆外一扔：「马家的东西，也敢吃？明儿马三一看是头大公鹿，你这张嘴，就是沈家的祸！」那块桂花糕落在篱笆根底下，小满隔着篱笆瞧了半天，到底没捡。
story_full.en:
And just then Yinyue said in his ear, ⟪"Half an inch to the left."⟫

Her voice was very soft and very tired, as if it had drifted from a long, long way off. Xiaoman moved half an inch left.

The reeds were nearly upright but not quite. His fingers let go.

The arrow was off the string with a *whoosh*, and before he could see where it went, his shoulder suddenly felt light. The little silver fox slid off his neck and dropped, limp. He threw down the bow and caught it — its eyes were shut, its body cold as a lump of ice. Last night it had been burning hot, and hot at least meant alive. Xiaoman panicked, stuffed it inside his jacket and held it against his chest, and felt that it was still breathing, very, very slowly.

He opened his mouth. He wanted to say "thanks", or "thank you", or something — anyway, something with a thank in it. The words were already on the tip of his tongue, but its eyes were shut, and it couldn't hear any more.

The stag by the stream, though, didn't fall. With the arrow hanging from its neck it leapt, bounded over the stream, and plunged into the wood on the far bank. His father grabbed Old Zhou, who was about to give chase: "Don't. Chase it, and it'll run further." Then he shut his eyes and listened for as long as it takes to smoke a pipe before he said, "It can't run any more. Follow the stream down, two hundred paces, there's a bend."

The three of them went down along the stream. After a full two hundred paces the water turned a bend, and on the shallows in the bend the stag lay on its side, the arrow right through its neck, dead on the mark. It had run this far, and only here had it fallen.

His father ran over, limping, ran faster than Old Zhou, and dropped to his knees beside the deer with a thump — knee forgotten — reached out to touch the antlers, and turned round to look at his son, grinning like a child. Xiaoman grinned too.

But his hand stayed pressed to his chest the whole time, and he didn't dare take it away.

Old Zhou looked at the deer, then at Xiaoman. "One arrow?" Xiaoman's father said, "One arrow." Old Zhou said, "He's only twelve." His father said, "I didn't touch this bow till I was fourteen. Nor did my father." He bent his head and stroked the stag's neck with his palm, stroke after stroke. Then he said, "He's twelve."

He said nothing more. But the voice he said those two words in was not the voice he'd said "Third Master" to Ma San in.

The door hadn't been lugged up for nothing after all: it carried a deer. His father insisted on taking the back end, and wouldn't listen to anyone. Xiaoman walked last, bow on his back, hand on his chest. The thing against his chest didn't move once the whole way.

By the time they reached the village gate it was evening.

Under the old locust tree stood two people. One was Ahe, both toes planted side by side against the roots of the old locust tree, her body leaning out in front, her neck stretched like a goose waiting to be fed. Her mother wouldn't let her past the village gate, and the old locust tree was the village gate. Not one of her feet had gone past it. Her neck already had.

The other person standing under the old locust tree was Xiaoman's mother. She had stood there from nightfall the day before right through to this evening, and had gone home only once in between, to put a handful of wood on the stove — in case they came back and found the stove cold. That would never do.

At the back of the crowd that gathered round to look at the deer, Beansprout Liu took one look at it, turned, and ran off towards the Ma place.

His mother came up to her son. First she looked at his face, then at his swollen left wrist. It was wrapped in half a strip of shirt hem, long since soaked by mud and water into a rotten rag. She didn't say a word. She undid the rag, tore a clean strip from under the hem of her own jacket, and wrapped it on again, round and round, and tied it off in a knot, neat and square, exactly like the knots she tied when she mended clothes.

Then she turned and looked at Xiaoman's father. He was carrying the back end of the door; the mud on his face wasn't washed off yet, and his eyes were as red as a rabbit's. The two of them looked at each other, and neither said anything. She reached out and picked a pine needle off his shoulder.

Just that, once.

That night Ma Xiaobao stopped Ahe by the well platform and traded her a piece of osmanthus cake for talk. "Beansprout Liu says the Shens brought back a great big deer. Was it really that big?" Ahe said, "He saw wrong. A little doe with a lame leg. Otherwise how could Shen Xiaoman have hit it?" Ma Xiaobao thought this made a great deal of sense, pushed the cake into her hand and left. Old Zhou came rushing out of the door, snatched the cake from her and threw it over the fence. "You'd eat something from the Mas? Tomorrow when Ma San sees it's a big stag, that mouth of yours will be the ruin of the Shens!" The osmanthus cake landed at the foot of the fence. Xiaoman looked at it through the fence for a long time, and in the end he didn't pick it up.

refuse.zh: 风还没歇。先看风，后看鹿。
refuse.en: The wind hasn't rested. Wind first, then the deer.

exits.means: ignores the wind and shoots straight

story.zh:
小满没理那句话。风？风懂什么。他照直放了箭。

箭擦着鹿角飞了过去，「笃」地钉进了溪对岸的泥里，尾羽还在晃。那头雄鹿猛地抬起头来，往四下里看了看，没看见人，只看见一支插在泥里、还在摇头晃脑的箭。它喷了一口白气，倒像在笑话这支箭，又低下头去，接着喝水。

他爹没说话，从箭壶里抽出第二支箭，递了过来。他肩上那团银毛，很轻很轻地，哼了一声。
story.en:
Xiaoman ignored it. Wind? What does the wind know. He loosed straight.

The arrow grazed the antlers and stuck *thock* in the mud across the stream, fletching still quivering. The stag's head came up; it looked all round, saw no one, only an arrow standing in the mud, still wagging its head. It snorted a white breath, as though laughing at the arrow, and lowered its head to drink again.

His father said nothing; he drew a second arrow from the quiver and handed it over. The silver fur on his shoulder gave a very, very small *hmph*.
